v.q: Which workload clearly favours a relational (SQL) database?
o: Money transfers needing multi-row transactions and strict constraints
Storing billions of independent sensor readings
Caching session tokens with automatic expiry
Storing large video files for streaming
v.w: SQL offers ACID transactions, joins and constraints, which suits ledgers. Other stores suit other shapes of data.

v.q: Which workload suits a relational database?
o: A banking ledger
Raw sensor log storage
Session token caching
Video file streaming
v.w: Money needs transactions, constraints and joins.

v.q: What best describes a document database such as MongoDB?
o: Self-contained JSON-like documents with a flexible schema
Fixed-width rows that are always held in rigid tables
Relationships stored as nodes and edges with properties
Plain key and value strings that are held only in memory
v.w: Documents suit data that is read and written as a whole, such as a product or user profile with nested fields.

v.q: Which statement about document databases is NOT true?
o: Every document must have the same fixed columns
Documents are JSON-like
Schemas can vary between documents
Related data can be embedded
v.w: Flexible schema is a main selling point.

v.q: Which store fits a very fast lookup of a value by key, such as a session or a rate-limit counter?
o: A key-value store such as Redis
A graph database
A column-family warehouse
A relational data mart
v.w: Key-value stores give very low latency for simple access patterns but limited querying beyond the key.

v.q: Which store gives sub-millisecond lookups by key?
o: Redis
A data warehouse
A graph database
A search index
v.w: An in-memory key-value store is built for simple fast access.

v.q: Which store fits finding friends-of-friends or detecting fraud rings?
o: A graph database such as Neo4j
A key-value store such as Redis
A document store such as MongoDB
A time-series database such as InfluxDB
v.w: Traversing relationships is the core strength of graphs. In SQL such queries need many self-joins.

v.q: Which question suits a graph database?
o: Which accounts share devices?
What is the balance of account 42?
List the last 10 transactions
Store this session token
v.w: Relationship traversal is the strength of graph stores.

v.q: Why do many NoSQL stores scale writes horizontally more easily?
o: They shard by key and give up cross-shard joins and transactions
They store far less data on each of the nodes in a cluster
They ignore durability entirely to gain more write speed
They keep only a single copy of the data to save disk space
v.w: Partitioning by key spreads load across nodes. Queries must fit the partition key, so design the data model around access patterns.

v.q: Which feature do many NoSQL stores give up to scale writes?
o: Cross-shard transactions
Storing data on disk
Using primary keys
Running on several nodes
v.w: Sharding by key makes distributed joins and transactions expensive or unavailable.

v.q: What is the main modelling difference between SQL and NoSQL?
o: SQL models data first, NoSQL often models around queries
SQL has no schema at all, while NoSQL always has a strict one
NoSQL is not able to store any relationships between records
NoSQL always enforces foreign keys between its collections
v.w: In document and wide-column stores you often duplicate data to serve each read pattern efficiently, trading storage and update complexity.

v.q: Which design approach is typical for NoSQL?
o: Model around the queries
Normalise to third normal form
Avoid duplication at any cost
Design tables before knowing the access pattern
v.w: The access patterns come first, and data is shaped to serve them.

v.q: A team picks MongoDB just because it is "schema-less". What is the usual consequence?
o: The schema moves into application code, and messy data can build up
No schema ever needs to exist anywhere in the system again
The data becomes consistent automatically as time passes
Every query becomes faster without any extra design work
v.w: Flexibility is helpful, but readers of the data still depend on its shape. Validate with schema rules and migrations.

v.q: Which statement about a schema-less database is NOT true?
o: No schema exists anywhere
The schema moves into code
Messy data can build up
Migration is still needed for changes
v.w: There is always an implicit schema, held by the application.

o: Using different data stores for different needs in one system
Writing SQL in several languages
Replicating one database across many regions
Storing the same data in every database
v.w: For example PostgreSQL for the ledger, Redis for sessions, Elasticsearch for search. The cost is more systems to operate and sync.

o: Postgres for payments and Redis for sessions
Three copies of one Postgres database
A single store for everything
Reports in several languages
v.w: Each data store is chosen for its job.
